> Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is absurd.
>
> — Voltaire, letter to Frederick II of Prussia, 6 April 1767 ("Le doute
> n'est pas un état bien agréable, mais l'assurance est un état ridicule.")

> To believe in anything for certain is a leap of faith.
>
> — *Philosophize This!*, [Episode #041, "Belief"](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2zh2SLNlD7b3yXIdcGRKca),
> hosted by Stephen West

There are two criteria for saying that a person believes a proposition. By the
first, **reflective judgment**, they believe it if, when they consider the
question, they judge it true and would sincerely assert it. By the second,
**dispositional belief**, they believe it if they are disposed to act, feel and
reason as though it were true. The two usually agree. These notes concern the
cases where they do not, which raise two questions: which of the two attitudes
counts as the belief, and which should give way to the other.

## Two Cases

- **Free will.** I am not persuaded that free will exists, in the sense of
  being able to have chosen otherwise than I did. My conduct presupposes that
  it does: I deliberate as though the outcome were open, hold myself
  responsible for what I choose, and feel gratitude and resentment toward
  others for what they choose.
- **AI risk.** I judge it plausible that advanced AI will cause a serious
  catastrophe within a few years. My conduct presupposes that it will not: I
  am still being a dad and living normally, and I plan as though the near
  future will resemble the present.

## Accounts of the Divergence

- **Alief.** Tamar Gendler, "Alief and Belief" (*Journal of Philosophy*,
  2008). An alief is an automatic, associative attitude, triggered by features
  of the immediate situation, that produces a feeling and an inclination to
  act. It can contradict a belief the person holds at the same moment.
  Gendler's example is the glass walkway over the Grand Canyon: a visitor
  believes the walkway will hold, aliefs that it will not, and trembles.
  Aliefs are changed by habituation and repeated exposure more readily than by
  evidence or argument.
- **Belief as a disposition to act.** Alexander Bain, in *The Emotions and the
  Will* (1859), defined belief as "that upon which a man is prepared to act".
  Charles Sanders Peirce built on that definition in "How to Make Our Ideas
  Clear" (1878), where he wrote that "the essence of belief is the
  establishment of a habit", and in 1907 he called pragmatism "scarce more
  than a corollary" of Bain's definition. By this criterion the attitude that
  governs conduct is the belief, and an assertion that conduct does not
  support is something less.
- **In-between belief.** Eric Schwitzgebel, "In-Between Believing"
  (*Philosophical Quarterly*, 2001) and "Acting Contrary to Our Professed
  Beliefs" (*Pacific Philosophical Quarterly*, 2010). Belief is a cluster of
  dispositions, and when some of the dispositions point one way and some the
  other, the person is neither accurately described as believing nor as
  disbelieving. His 2010 example is a professor who sincerely judges that all
  races are equally intelligent and whose spontaneous judgments of individual
  students are racially biased.
- **Somatic markers.** Antonio Damasio, *Descartes' Error* (1994). Bodily
  states associated with the past outcomes of similar choices bias decisions,
  and narrow the options considered, before and during explicit reasoning.
  Damasio's evidence is patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal
  cortex, who reason through a choice normally and still choose badly.

## Free Will

- **Hume and backgammon.** In the conclusion to Book 1 of *A Treatise of Human
  Nature* (1739), Hume's skeptical arguments leave him unable to trust reason,
  and the doubt does not survive ordinary life: "I dine, I play a game of
  back-gammon, I converse, and am merry with my friends; and when after three
  or four hours' amusement, I wou'd return to these speculations, they appear
  so cold, and strain'd, and ridiculous, that I cannot find in my heart to
  enter into them any farther." The passage concerns his skepticism about
  reason in general, not free will specifically; it is cited here as the
  classic description of a reflective conclusion that conduct does not follow.
  Hume's own position on free will, in Book 2 of the *Treatise* and Section 8
  of the *Enquiry*, is that liberty and necessity are compatible.
- **Reactive attitudes.** P. F. Strawson, "Freedom and Resentment"
  (*Proceedings of the British Academy*, 1962). Resentment, gratitude, blame
  and love are constitutive of relationships between people, and the
  commitment to them is too deeply rooted for a general theoretical conviction
  such as determinism to remove. Strawson argues further that even if giving
  them up were possible, the choice would rightly be made on what it would do
  to human life, not on whether determinism is true.
- **Acting under the idea of freedom.** Immanuel Kant, *Groundwork of the
  Metaphysics of Morals* (1785), Section III: a being that cannot act except
  under the idea of freedom is, in a practical respect, free. Deliberation
  presupposes that the outcome is open, whatever the metaphysical facts.

## Catastrophe and Ordinary Life

- **C. S. Lewis, "On Living in an Atomic Age" (1948).** Collected in *Present
  Concerns* (1986). Lewis observes that everyone was already under sentence of
  death before the bomb was invented, and that earlier generations lived
  through plague and war. If the bomb comes, he wants it to find people
  "doing sensible and human things", such as working, reading and bathing the
  children, "not huddled together like frightened sheep and thinking about
  bombs."
- **Luther's apple tree.** "Even if I knew that tomorrow the world would go to
  pieces, I would still plant my apple tree." The saying is attributed to
  Martin Luther but appears nowhere in his writings. Its earliest documented
  use is a circular letter of 5 October 1944 by Karl Lotz, a pastor of the
  Confessing Church in Hesse, who already treated it as a known saying of
  Luther's.
- **Workability.** [Acceptance and Commitment
  Therapy](acceptance-and-commitment-therapy.qmd) evaluates a thought by
  whether acting on it serves the person's values, and sets aside whether the
  thought is true. Applied here, the forecast can be held as possibly correct
  while conduct is governed by values.

## Questions to Sit With

- **When does the divergence have a cost?** Only when the reflective judgment,
  if it governed conduct, would produce different actions. Determinism
  prescribes no different action, since a choice still has to be made, so the
  divergence over free will costs nothing. For AI risk the test is what I
  would do differently if my conduct followed my judgment. If the answer is
  little beyond what I already do, judgment and conduct agree on the action
  and diverge only in feeling.
- **Which attitude should give way?** In Gendler's example the reflective
  belief is correct and the alief is the error. In the AI case either could be
  the error: the judgment may be right and the calm a failure to update, or
  the calm may be tracking something the judgment overstates. The distinction
  between the two attitudes does not settle which; the evidence for the
  proposition does.
- **Can argument change a dispositional belief?** Gendler's account, and the
  practice of exposure therapy, suggest that it mostly cannot, and that
  repeated experience does. The converse question is whether a reflective
  judgment should be revised when conduct will not follow it.
